newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk police say Nadir safe from British officials.
newsitem.headline: Turk police say Nadir safe from British officials.

text.p: Turkish police said on Tuesday they would not hand over to British authorities the Turkish Cypriot fugitive tycoon Asil Nadir who is on a business trip in Istanbul.
"It is not possible for a Turkish citizen to be extradited to the country in question, no matter what his crime may be," Anatolian news agency quoted senior policeman Ihsan Yilmazturk as saying.
But a lawyer for Nadir, Ali Riza Gorgun, suggested there was a possibility that Nadir would return to Britain voluntarily.
"Of course he could return but at the moment we are enjoying the feeling of freedom," Gorgun told journalists waiting outside Nadir's hotel by Istanbul's Bosphorus Strait.
Nadir, who also holds a Turkish passport, flew to Turkey on business on Monday in his first trip out of his native north Cyprus since he fled there from British justice four years ago.
He jumped bail in Britain in May, 1993 while awaiting trial on theft and false accounting charges related to the collapse of his Polly Peck lemons-to-electronics empire.
Speaking from the balcony of his hotel room, Nadir made only a short comment to reporters waiting below.
"I came to serve my country and complete business that I left half finished in the past," he said.
Aides did not say what the nature of Nadir's business in Turkey was.
Yilmazturk, the head of the Turkish police's Interpol division, told Anatolian he had already informed British police that no action would be taken against Nadir in Turkey.
Britain and NATO ally Turkey do not have an extradition treaty but usually hand over criminal suspects to each other under a Council of Europe agreement.
The British embassy in Ankara said earlier it hoped Turkish police would arrest the fallen magnate on the strength of an Interpol "wanted" notice.

"We would expect the Turkish police to detain him as there is an Interpol red notice against him," an embassy spokesman said. "We have reminded the Turkish authorities of the existence of this notice on a number of occasions."
The London Times said earlier this month that policemen acting for the Serious Fraud Office had been sent to Turkey to seek Nadir's arrest after the businessman said he would fly to Istanbul.
